msDesc.head: A Persianate South Asian album of ten folios, with five paintings and drawings as well as five calligraphy specimens.

msContents.summary: This Persianate South Asian album of ten folios preserves five paintings and drawings, as well as five Persian calligraphy specimens. A majority of the folios bear the seal impression of Sir Elijah Impey (1732–1809), who served as Chief Justice in Calcutta between 1774 to 1783, during which time, he amassed a considerable collection of manuscripts, drawings, and antiquarian objects.

supportDesc.support: The first double-sided, appended leaf excepted, all folios appear prepared and uniformly mounted onto the same underlying heavy-weight paper, left blank.
supportDesc.condition: Handle with caution, Folios in fair condition, with abrasion and delamination along the for-edge.

physDesc.additions: Bookplates: The left pastedown: Bibliotheca Lindesiana with shelfmark 4/A, Bland MSS No. 75.

binding.p: Pamphlet-stitched through a three rectangular strips of paper. Case-bound in full, green silk striped brocade Endpapers of brilliant pink, early-19th century, coated wove paper. The same appears on Persian MS 51.
binding.condition: Handle with caution. Spine completed abraded away and delaminating from the front boards.

seal.p:
Rectangular seal impressions, intaglio carved in nasta‘līq script in two stacked lines, double-ruled, of former owner Sir Elijah Impey (1732–1809), dated 1775, along with a regnal year 16 of George III, King of Great Britain (b. 1738, r. 1760–1820) reads from bottom upwards:
سر ایلاجه ایمپی چیف جستس سنه ۱۶، ۱۷۷۵
(Sir Īlāhah Īmpī Chīf Justis, sanah 16, 1775).
Dimensions:
19 26

history.origin: The content originates from different periods and sources, which an artist formed into an album either assembled for, or acquired by, Sir Elijah Impey (1732–1809) in Calcutta (Kolkata), as per his seal impressions. Impey served as the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William between 1774 to 1783, where he amassed a considerable collection, before he returned to Britain and passed away.

provenance.p: The London firm of Harry Phillips (d. 1840) sold Impey's collection 21 May 1810, including five albums of ten folios, Nº 279–283.

Probably subsequently acquired by Methodist minister Rev. Adam Clarke (1762–1832), after whose death his son Jospeh Butterworth Bulmer Clarke (d. 1855) inherited the volume and describes its present state in a catalogue published in 1835.

The next year on 20 June 1836, Clarke's son auctioned his father's collection through the London firm of Sotheby & Son, Nº 147, where bookseller William Straker purchased it for £5 15 shillings and sixpence.
Probably sold by Straker to scholar Nathaniel Bland (1803–1865) for his library at Randalls Park, Leatherhead.

After Bland's death, London bookseller Bernard Quaritch (1819–1899) sold his oriental manuscripts to Alexander Lindsay, 25th Earl of Crawford (1812–1880) in June, 1866, paid in two instalments of £450 and £400, and then moved to Bibliotheca Lindesiana at Haigh Hall, Wigan.
Purchased by Enriqueta Rylands (1843–1908) in 1901 from James Ludovic Lindsay, 26th Earl of Crawford (1847–1913).

acquisition.p: Bequeathed by Enriqueta Rylands (1843–1908) in 1908 to the John Rylands Library, Manchester.

source.p: Bibliographical description based on a manuscript catalogue by Michael Kerney, circa 1890s.
Manuscript description by Jake Benson in 2026 with reference to the volume in hand.

msContents.summary: Safavid-era calligrapher, Mu‘izz al-Dīn Muḥammad al-Ḥusaynī (fl. late 16th c) of Kashan, copied this excerpt from a ghazal (lyric) poem composed by Amīr Shāhī Sabzavārī, d. 1453 as a quatrain, in 986 AH (1578–1579 CE).

msItem.title: Quatrain derived from a ghazal
msItem.quote: ای پیک دیار آشنایی * از غایب ما خبر چه داری؟ | گفتی، ستم فراق سهلست * بسم الله، از این بتر چه داری؟
msItem.colophon: Completed by Mu‘izz al-Dīn Muḥammad al-Ḥusaynī in 986 AH (1578–1579 CE).

supportDesc.support:
Central calligraphy written on a buff-coloured paper, decorated with a finely sprayed positive-cut stencil of pale pink, featuring serrated sāz foliate scrollwork outlined in gold, sized and polished. Adhered to stacked, quadruple 'post-and-lintel' mounts comprised of blue and yellow-tinted, finely gold-flecked interior margins, surrounded by a wider dark indigo blue margin featuring hand-painted gilt foliate scrollwork, mounted onto a wide buff-coloured gold-flecked margin, then inset within a comparatively narrow outer frame of machine-made wove paper, identical to the endpapers. The last excepted, all of the stocks appear probably handmade in India.

msContents.summary: A detached folio from an anthology features a ghazal (lyric) poem of Sa‘dī (ca. 1213–1292).

msItem.title: Ghazal
msItem.quote: بازآی که از غم تو ما را * چشمی و هزار چشمه آب است | تندی و جفا و زشت‌خویی * هرچند که می‌کنی نکویی | فرمان برمت به هر چه گویی * جان بر لب و چشم بر خطاب است | ای روی تو از بهشت بابی * دل بر نمک لبت کبابی | گفتم بزنم بر آتش آبی * وین آتش دل نه جای آب است | ای سرو روان و گلبن نو * مه پیکرِ آفتاب‌پرتو | بستان و بده؛ بگوی و بشنو * شب‌های چنین نه وقت خواب است | این گُرسِنه‌گرگِ بی‌ترحم * خود سیر نمی‌شود ز مردم | ابنای زمان مثال گندم * وین دور فلک چو آسیاب است | سعدی تو نه مرد وصل اویی * تا لاف زنی و قرب جویی | از هرچه می‌رود، سخنِ دوست خوش‌تر است * پیغام آشنا، نفَسِ روح‌پرور است
